pointers.sentence: In 5.1 the parser gained `Parser.extra_data`, a dictionary in which a tag's compile function may leave data, kept as `Template.extra_data` once the parse succeeds (`django/template/base.py:Template.compile_nodelist`); partials (6.0) are built on it.

`{% partialdef row %}` … `{% endpartialdef %}` files a `PartialTemplate` there under `"partials"`, and renders nothing where it stands unless the tag adds `"inline"` (`django/template/defaulttags.py:partialdef_func`); `{% partial row %}` renders the fragment in the context at that point (`django/template/defaulttags.py:PartialNode.render`).

`{% partialdef row %}` … `{% endpartialdef %}` files a `PartialTemplate` there under `"partials"`, and renders nothing where it stands unless the tag adds `"inline"` (`django/template/defaulttags.py:partialdef_func`); `{% partial row %}` renders the fragment in the context at that point (`django/template/defaulttags.py:PartialNode.render`).

A name such as `"entries.html#row"`, given to `Engine.get_template` and so to `render_to_string` and `{% include %}`, is split at its first `"#"`: the template before it is loaded, and the partial filed under the rest returned (`django/template/engine.py:Engine.get_template`).
The 6.0 notes give the purpose, "to encapsulate and reuse small named fragments within a template file", and a guide for users of django-template-partials (`docs/releases/6.0.txt`).
In `{{ entry..title }}` the empty name between the dots is looked up like any other part (`django/template/base.py:Variable._resolve_lookup`).

6.1 deprecated the form, "normally a mistake" in its notes (`docs/releases/6.1.txt`): `Parser.parse` warns as it compiles a variable tag whose variable holds two dots in a row, and a comment there says it becomes an error when the deprecation ends, in Django 2028 (`django/template/base.py:Parser.parse`).

6.1 deprecated the form, "normally a mistake" in its notes (`docs/releases/6.1.txt`): `Parser.parse` warns as it compiles a variable tag whose variable holds two dots in a row, and a comment there says it becomes an error when the deprecation ends, in Django 2028 (`django/template/base.py:Parser.parse`).

A literal is not checked (`FilterExpression.is_var`): `{{ "a..b" }}` warns under neither 6.1.1 nor this commit, 6.1.1 having stopped 6.1's warning for them (`docs/releases/6.1.1.txt`; [Variables and filters: `FilterExpression` and `Variable`](../templates/variables.md)).

`{% if entry..title %}` compiles without a warning under 5.2.17 and every release since, its condition false, and `Parser.parse` does not look at a filter's argument such as `default:entry..title`, which fails only at render (`django/template/base.py:FilterExpression.resolve`).

Until then `parse_bits`, which matches a tag's words to the function's signature as a template compiles, was given that flag; the 6.1 notes say only that the undocumented function no longer accepts it (`docs/releases/6.1.txt`), and an old call with it is a `TypeError` from 6.1.1, with no warning before.

Each of the decorators `Library.simple_tag`, `Library.simple_block_tag` and `Library.inclusion_tag` now checks that the function's first parameter is `"context"`, and strikes it, as it decorates the function (`django/template/library.py:Library.simple_tag`):
`{% querystring %}`, new in 5.1, writes a link's query string from the request's parameters and the template's, where a template had looped over them (`docs/releases/5.1.txt`).

6.0 let it take several positional mappings, applied in order before the keyword arguments, and made the result always begin with `"?"` (`django/template/defaulttags.py:querystring`): on a request for `"/entries/"`, `{% querystring %}` wrote nothing under 5.2.17 and `"?"` from 6.0.8, and two mappings, which 5.2.17 refused at compile time ("received too many positional arguments"), make one query string from 6.0.8 ([The built-in tags](../templates/tags.md)).

A callable that a variable's lookup finds is not called if it carries a true `"alters_data"`; the value becomes the engine's `"string_if_invalid"` (`django/template/base.py:Variable._resolve_lookup`).

5.2 set the flag on `QuerySet.create`, `QuerySet.bulk_create`, `QuerySet.get_or_create`, `QuerySet.update_or_create`, `UserManager.create_user`, `UserManager.create_superuser` and their coroutine twins, "to prevent side effects when rendering a template context" (`docs/releases/5.2.txt`).

A manager's copies, made with `functools.wraps`, carry it too (`django/db/models/manager.py:BaseManager._get_queryset_methods`): with a manager as entries, `{{ entries.create }}` renders the empty string under 5.2.17, which already carries 5.2's change, and every release since.
`format_html` passes each argument through `conditional_escape` and marks the result safe (`django/utils/html.py:format_html`), so a call with nothing to format would mark its text safe unexamined.

`urlize`, behind the filters `|urlize` and `|urlizetrunc`, links a name without a scheme that begins `"www."` or whose domain ends in one of the seven original top-level domains, and gives it `"http://"`, or `"https://"` when the transitional setting `URLIZE_ASSUME_HTTPS` is true (`django/utils/html.py:Urlizer.handle_word`).
6.0 deprecated the default, which Django 2028 makes `"https://"`, removing the setting (`docs/internals/deprecation.txt`).
The 6.0 notes call the setting deprecated, but nothing warns when it is set (`docs/releases/6.0.txt`, `django/conf/__init__.py:Settings.__init__`).
